The rider's consent extends only to a stop: at 21:35 the driver asked permission to 'pull in at the petrol station just ahead for one minute' and at 21:36 the rider replied 'Sure, no problem' — a general permission to stop, not a route authorisation, and it names no road and no detour, so under RD-5 it cannot cover the 6.27 km loop (the rider also confirms no petrol stop occurred).

The driver's after-the-fact statement that 'the rider agreed to a short stop so I thought a small change of route was fine' is a unilateral widening of the rider's consent and, being only the driver's assertion of agreement, does not constitute consent under RD-5.

Because this is a RydeTAXI metered trip, the unexempted detour mileage flowed directly into the fare: the fare record bills excess distance of $6.77 (4.80 km × $1.4100/km), and the rider should recover the excess mileage attributable to the off-route segment.

The waiting charge of $0.11 (0.4 min × $0.26/min) is a metered waiting unit on a RydeTAXI trip and is chargeable under RD-3(c), so it is not part of the refund sought; the claim is confined to the detour mileage.
The driver already has 2 upheld disputes in the last 90 days and this route deviation, if upheld, makes it repeated conduct, which supports the additional action of sending the account for review.

weaknesses: The rider did consent to a stop (F8, F9), so the driver will argue the whole 21:39–21:49 deviation was within the agreed 'small change of route' (F11) — our answer is that the message names only a petrol station 'just ahead' and one minute, reaching nowhere near 4.56 km and 1958 m (F3), but the judge must read the words.

The rider's consent message (F9) is a general 'Sure, no problem' with no named road, and no fact ties the driven segment to any specifically agreed road, so on the RD-5 'named road' branch the judge may find the reach of the consent undetermined (G13), which would send the amount to a human.

The refund figure is not directly stated in any single fact: RD-2's formula (unexempted extra_km × distance fare ÷ distance km) applied to F3's 4.56 km and F4's $1.41/km gives $6.43, which is less than the full billed excess of $6.77 in F4, so the driver can argue the extra $0.34 (matching-noise mileage) is not refundable under RD-2.

The driver's 90-day dispute history (F17: 4 disputes, 2 upheld) shows no prior route disputes, so a rider-side flag_account argument rests on thin ground, and flag_account cannot be the main finding (RD-6).

claims.assertion: The trip ran 18.7 km against an optimal 13.9 km, i.e. +4.8 km (+35%), so the driver did not take the shortest and most direct route as RD-1 requires.

The GPS track identifies one off-route segment (21:39–21:49) covering 6.27 km where the optimal route covers 1.71 km, adding 4.56 km and reaching up to 1958 m from the optimal route — a non-exempt deviation under RD-1.

This deviation was not justified by traffic: no incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, and the only speed-band records on the corridor (CExpressway and Kampong Bahru Road, band 5, 40–49 km/h) are nowhere near the band 1–2 severe-congestion range, so RD-4(a) is not met and RD-4(b) cannot exempt the segment on its own.

The rider's consent extends only to a stop: at 21:35 the driver asked permission to 'pull in at the petrol station just ahead for one minute' and at 21:36 the rider replied 'Sure, no problem' — a general permission to stop, not a route authorisation, and it names no road and no detour, so under RD-5 it cannot cover the 6.27 km loop (the rider also confirms no petrol stop occurred).

The driver's after-the-fact statement that 'the rider agreed to a short stop so I thought a small change of route was fine' is a unilateral widening of the rider's consent and, being only the driver's assertion of agreement, does not constitute consent under RD-5.

Because this is a RydeTAXI metered trip, the unexempted detour mileage flowed directly into the fare: the fare record bills excess distance of $6.77 (4.80 km × $1.4100/km), and the rider should recover the excess mileage attributable to the off-route segment.

The waiting charge of $0.11 (0.4 min × $0.26/min) is a metered waiting unit on a RydeTAXI trip and is chargeable under RD-3(c), so it is not part of the refund sought; the claim is confined to the detour mileage.
The driver already has 2 upheld disputes in the last 90 days and this route deviation, if upheld, makes it repeated conduct, which supports the additional action of sending the account for review.

weaknesses: The rider did consent to a stop (F8, F9), so the driver will argue the whole 21:39–21:49 deviation was within the agreed 'small change of route' (F11) — our answer is that the message names only a petrol station 'just ahead' and one minute, reaching nowhere near 4.56 km and 1958 m (F3), but the judge must read the words.

The rider's consent message (F9) is a general 'Sure, no problem' with no named road, and no fact ties the driven segment to any specifically agreed road, so on the RD-5 'named road' branch the judge may find the reach of the consent undetermined (G13), which would send the amount to a human.

The refund figure is not directly stated in any single fact: RD-2's formula (unexempted extra_km × distance fare ÷ distance km) applied to F3's 4.56 km and F4's $1.41/km gives $6.43, which is less than the full billed excess of $6.77 in F4, so the driver can argue the extra $0.34 (matching-noise mileage) is not refundable under RD-2.

The driver's 90-day dispute history (F17: 4 disputes, 2 upheld) shows no prior route disputes, so a rider-side flag_account argument rests on thin ground, and flag_account cannot be the main finding (RD-6).

claims.assertion: The rider personally authorised the driver to leave the direct route before the deviation began: chat #2 (F9, 21:36) reads 'Sure, no problem.' in reply to the driver's request at 21:35 (F8) to pull in at a petrol station 'just ahead', i.e. before the off-route segment started at 21:39 (F3).

The consent in F9 was only a general permission for a short stop, not a named-road consent, and no fact ties the 21:39–21:49 driven segment to any particular road, so under RD-5 the reach of that consent is undetermined rather than a blanket exemption.

The rider never named a location for the stop and no chat message identifies the petrol station or the route, so the driver's own statement that he 'thought a small change of route was fine' (F11) cannot extend the rider's consent to the whole 4.56 km detour; RD-3(b) leaves that segment's extra_km unexempted.

No reasonable-cause defence is available: the only traffic records are speed band 5 (40–49 km/h) on CEP and Kampong Bahru Road (F12, F13, not bands 1–2) and F14 records no incident near the optimal route, so RD-4 does not exempt the segment.

This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (F7 total $39.18 metered), so only the metered distance units attributable to the unexempted segment are refundable: 4.56 km × $1.41/km = $6.43, computed from F3's extra_km and F4's per-km rate of $1.4100.
The $0.11 waiting fee is meter waiting time of 0.4 min (F5) recorded during a RydeTAXI trip and is therefore chargeable, not refundable, under RD-3(c).
